does: Folds a sheet or a round of dough over itself, from the sides and into a square or a letter, so that it stacks into layers or gains strength, and so that any fat or oil brushed between the layers stays shut in them.

intro.what: Rested dough is spread into a sheet and folded over itself in the shape the dish requires.
intro.why: Folding can build structure and stack layers. When the dish uses fat between folds, complete coverage and gentle handling preserve that separation.

how: Rest the dough first, so that it relaxes and does not spring back.
Stretch or roll it into an even sheet on a lightly oiled or floured surface.
Brush or sprinkle the surface with the fat or the dusting the dish asks for, right to the edges.
Lift one edge and fold it over towards the middle, then bring the opposite edge over it, as when folding a letter. For a square, fold the other sides in as well.
Press the folded shape lightly, turn it, and rest it before it is rolled or stretched again.

cues.text: The layers show along a cut edge as fine, even lines.
The dough is supple and springs back slowly, and tears only when it is pulled hard.

mistakes.mistake: Folding dough that is still tense, which tears and shrinks back.
mistakes.fix: Let it rest until it relaxes.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the corners and edges bare, so that the layers weld together there.
mistakes.fix: Brush the fat right to the edges.

quiz.question: What can folding create in a layered dough?
choices: A thicker sheet with the layers pressed firmly together.
Stacked sheets with the prescribed fat between them.
A tightly rolled strand with no sheet-like layers.
quiz.because: Folding stacks the dough surfaces; separating fat keeps those surfaces from simply joining.

quiz.question: What should happen before stretching tense dough?
choices: Pull harder while it springs back.
Fold it tightly without spreading it.
Let it rest until it relaxes.
quiz.because: Resting reduces the resistance that makes tense dough shrink or tear.

quiz.question: What can show that a layered fold has remained distinct?
choices: Fine even lines along a cut edge.
A solid fused edge without lines.
A ragged dry edge filled with holes.
quiz.because: Lines along the edge reveal the stacked sheets inside the dough.

quiz.question: The layers welded together at dry corners. What would you change next time?
choices: Leave a wider dry border around every fold.
Carry the prescribed fat to the edges before folding.
Press the dry corners together harder.
quiz.because: Fat coverage at the corners helps maintain separation there as well as at the centre.

comes_after.why: A dough is rolled or stretched into an even sheet before it is folded.
